utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Alex Demirdjian, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no housekeeping or similar matters, could the Usher please escort the witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one thing, if I may, before the witness is -- while the witness is ushered in. I failed to announce and I -- and I found out only right now, I failed to announce two documents which I would like to use at the beginning. Those are the charts prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor. The structure of the MUP, and the -- and the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know if there would be any opposition to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No opposition, Your Honour, except I haven't got them here. All right. We can arrange for someone to bring them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can borrow you mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or even lend it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Lend it, yes. Thank you. And I'm really sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could somebody remind me as to what the status is? Were they merely working documents or were they exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, they're admitted as exhibits, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Would you please make the solemn declaration from the card the Usher is now handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: From your responses to this point, I assume that you are hearing me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I will leave it to counsel at whose instance you are being called to lead you on evidence about particulars about yourself and your qualifications. I would, however, first of all, welcome you to this Tribunal and thank you for coming to give evidence. Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in any of the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been called by counsel for the accused Stanisic, and counsel would begin -- the procedure is that counsel -- the side -- counsel for the side calling you would begin by asking you questions following which the side opposite -- well, following which the side for the co-accused would have an opportunity to cross-examine you. Followed by counsel for the Prosecution, the side opposite. Counsel calling you would then have a right to re-examine you on matters that would have arisen out of cross-examination, and usually, at that stage but indeed at any stage the members of the Bench may put questions to you. It is estimated by counsel for the accused Stanisic that you will be on the witness-stand for a total of 20 hours. Counsel for the Prosecution has indicated that their cross-examination is likely to take the same period of time. Counsel for the co-accused, Mr. Zupljanin, have indicated that they would not be nearly as long with you, but all told, it will mean that you are expected to be before the Tribunal giving evidence for the remainder of this week and indeed for the next three weeks, according -- if I recall the schedule correctly. But from what I would have indicated in terms of the numbers of hours, you would have an idea as to how long your testimony is likely to take. You needn't be alarmed that you would be on the stand for 20 hours continuously. For technical reasons, the Tribunal's work is broken up into sessions of approximately 90 minutes and there are two reasons for this. One is the technical reason that the tapes that memorialise and record the proceedings have to be changed at approximately 90-minute intervals, and the secondary reason is that that allows for the comfort and convenience of witnesses, counsel, and everyone to take a break and then come back. Now, notwithstanding those set times that I have indicated, if, at any point in your testimony there is any reason that you would need to take a break, please indicate that to us, either directly or through your counsel, and it is something that we would, of course, accommodate. And unless you have any questions with which I may assist, I would invite counsel for Mr. Stanisic to begin their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, please tell us briefly something about yourself. Where you were born, what schools you graduated from and so on.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Derventa, and I have a degree in national defence from Belgrade university. And in early 1990, I worked in -- in the 1980s, I started working in secondary schools. Thereupon I went to work for the Secretariat for National Defence, and then, as of 1991, I started working for the MUP, and that's where I work to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, let me explain one matter to you. Since what you are saying is being interpreted, please speak slowly so that the interpreters have ample time to catch up with you? Tell us, please, the year of your birth and the place where you graduated from secondary and other schools?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1954. I completed my primary education in my native town, and the secondary school in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you graduated from the Faculty of National Defence in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that upon your graduation, you worked in a secondary school and then in the Secretariat for National Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain for us, what were the activities of the Secretariat for National Defence at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Secretariat for National Defence was structured, let me organise the hierarchy. There was the Federal Secretariat for National Defence which covered the whole of Yugoslavia. Then the Republican Secretariat for National Defence in each of the republics. And then at municipal level, there were Municipal Secretariats for National Defence which dealt with the recruitment and assignment of recruits to the JNA, the manning of JNA units and Territorial Defence units, the organisation of defence activities for all the other sectors of society at municipality level, mobilisation schedules for all the various structures, civilian protection, and engaged in certain forms of training in these particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the military records of conscripts were kept where exactly; and did they have anything to do with the secretariats for national defence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was precisely there that all the military records were kept at a certain territorial organisation unit, and it was there that at the request of certain wartime units and other authorities which dealt with the organisation of wartime matters that individuals were recruited. This was also the place where mobilisation was worked out, the way in which was to proceed, and it was already carried out, both the mobilisation of personnel and of assets, as well as of members of the civilian protection and all the other individuals who had specific wartime assignments. Furthermore, there were also emergency plans. All those were developed according to a uniform methodology that was prescribed by the Law on National Defence and a number of bylaws. They were to provide guide-lines and instructions, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please describe it quite plastically for Their Honours the issue of recruitment and how it worked. Were all conscripts, let's say, males of military age in a given, let's say, municipality, were they all listed as recruits; and at what point in their life would this be?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were males, as you yourself said, who, as they turned 18, would be listed in the military records and referred to recruitment commissions where they would undergo physical and psychological examinations to determine their fitness for military service. This was a sort of screening process, the aim of which was precisely to determine who, among those conscripts, was fit to do military service, and those who were declared unfit would be listed in special records, as precisely such individuals. The remainder who were deemed fit for military service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is one little thing which is not quite clear to me, Mr. Bjelosevic. Counsel Zecevic asked you whether the military records of the conscripts were kept where exactly and did they have to do anything with Secretariat for National Defence, and then your answer was, as it was recorded, that: "... it was precisely there that all the military records were kept ..." And my question is simply, was that at the federal level in Belgrade or were these records kept regionally in the various departments of the secretariat? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And that's precisely what I was about to talk about in my answer. I said that there was this screening process which took place, and once these individuals were listed in military records and these military records were kept at the level of Municipal Secretariat for -- Secretariats for National Defence, which, through the structure of Military Districts were sent on to the Republican Secretariats for National Defence and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. Next, in keeping with the wartime and peacetime plans for various units, a plan of war -- or, rather, a plan of assignments or posting of these various recruits to the JNA would be made, and this plan, from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, via the Republican Secretariats and Military Districts would be delivered to the various Municipal Secretariats for National Defence, and they would be the ones who would physically dispatch recruits to the destinations as determined by the structures higher up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, once the recruits completed their training in the Yugoslavia People's Army, they would, on their return, I assume, report again to the Secretariat for National Defence when they would be assigned to the reserve force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Their individual and unit files would be sent from the area where they served to their, let's call it home Secretariat for National Defence, and into these files it would be entered that they had completed their compulsory military service, their speciality and specific skills would also be listed in their files, and it was on that basis, and on the basis of the requirements in the army, their wartime assignments would be made. They would be assigned to either units or other structures, such as the police, territorial units, that's to say, units of the Territorial Defence, or units of the civilian protection. Alternatively, it could have been a wartime assignment to a certain company or institution. It all depended on the person's qualifications and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence would be the body which, if I understand you correctly, made specific assignments for individuals who had completed their compulsory military service. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And based on their files and skills acquired during their training in the Yugoslav People's Army, they would be assigned to the police reserve force, among others.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it is based on that that they would be assigned to various structures, including the police reserve force, depending on the number of police stations available and a number of other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, would the files of these individuals in that case be transferred to the Ministry of Interior or, as they were called, the secretariats of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. The master copy of their file would be kept with the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence. So the individual's file would be kept by the secretariat, whereas the file for the entire unit would be sent to the structure receiving the individual under this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the master copies of these files were always kept with the Secretariat for National Defence in the territory of the municipality where the individual resided; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, if I understand you well, the assignments after the person has finished his -- his military service, his normal military service, the assignments after that, are only wartime assignments; is that correct? So you were, for instance, in the -- in the reserve police only for wartime. You wouldn't be bothered by it in peacetime. Is that -- do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was wartime deployment, and stations of the so-called military police were established thereby. However, that composition was occasionally summoned primarily for further training and, secondly, in case of some exceptional circumstances or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, you've told us that at the Secretariat for National Defence you spent seven or nine years working there.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, you joined the MUP of the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have prepared a binder of documents to facilitate the -- for the witness so he can look at the whole document once it is shown to him so if -- if Usher can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, you started working at the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina when exactly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was in early May or perhaps the end of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you apply for a job? Was there a vacancy announced? How did you get the job?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The procedure that was in place for such appointments was a bit complicated, I would say. And I mean by that that there were supposed to be at least -- at least -- at least three candidates, or, rather, proposals for at least three candidates had to be submitted. After that, all the applicants were invited to undergo a physical examination, or, rather, their physical and mental abilities were tested. After the results came out, one of the three or more candidates were selected for the job in question. One of the conditions that a candidate had to meet was for the political parties that formed a coalition at that time endorsed the appointment of any such candidate. And those arrangements were usually made between the personnel commission of the MUP and a representative of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, was there also security check for each candidate?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That was a must. Let me just digress a little and tell you that if somebody was deployed into the police, they would be vetted. And for management staff, there were very detailed security checks. And, of course, that included checking references from a previous time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said, on page 12, point 1, that if somebody was transferred to the police force, you meant your job in the Secretariat for National Defence, and you meant when somebody was transferred to the police reserve, even then, there had to be security checks for such people, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in late April or early May, you became the chief of the Security Services Centre of Doboj, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call it up in e-court. It's 65 ter -- the Prosecutor's 65 ter 10137, paragraph 3, or item 3, which is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 65 ter 10137.3, which is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I apologise, this is not the map that I had in mind. Strike that. I don't need this document. The number must have been wrong or -- obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of the position of Doboj municipality, could you please provide us some detail about its geographical position, its placement in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doboj is in the northern or central northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the axis from Sarajevo to Slavonski Brod, on the river Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us how many municipal secretariats or public security stations at the moment when you were appointed the chief of the Security Services Centre in Doboj were there, and could you tell us which stations those were.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under the Doboj centre, there were the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please do it slowly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The public security station Brod; Derventa; Odzak; Samac; Modrica; Doboj; Tesanj; Teslic; and Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, there were nine public security stations within the framework of the Security Services Centre of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in 1991, who were the persons that were chiefs of those public security stations? Can you give us their names? Who were there in 1991? Who was appointed in 1991? Could you please do it slowly again. It is rather difficult to record the names.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, but I'll try and remember all of their names. In the Brod station, the person in charge was Slavko Pranjic. Later on, there was a shake-up, and he was replaced by Zvonko Nedanovic, I believe. In Odzak, it was Stjepan Mikic. In Samac, Vinko Dragicevic. In Modrica, the person's last name was Ibel and I'm not sure about his first name. I think it was Zvonko. In Doboj, Obren Petrovic. In Derventa, I found Novak Novic there, but he was soon removed and replaced by Ivan Duspara. In Maglaj, Osman Rahmanovic. I believe that that was the person's name. In Tesanj, Semsudin Mehmedovic. And in Teslic, Dusan Ismanovic [as interpreted]. I believe that I gave you all of their names correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the transcript, Obren Petrovic, page 14, line 1, he was chief of the police station in Doboj, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in Tesanj, the person's name was Semsudin Mehmedovic, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in Teslic, 14, 5, the person's name is Dusan Kuzmanovic. Sir, let's look at a document at tab 1; 752, document D1. 65 ter 00752D1. That's a Defence 65 ter, tab number 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe the document for us. Just briefly. What is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the regulation on internal organisation and the list of positions in the Secretariat of the Interior, as it was still known, in 1990. That regulation was in force in 1991 when I joined as the chief of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, that was the regulation on the internal organisation of the republican SUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was still valid, and it was still in effect at the time when you were appointed the chief of the Security Services Centre in Doboj, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this document also provides a description of the entire structure. For example, on page 59 you can see it. You see what the centre is made up of, what elements went into it, and it also gives you job descriptions of each of the organisational elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2? This the page that the gentleman was referring to. I'm interested in Article 59 on the following page of the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this -- what strikes me in the first page is that it is a proposal. It is said to be a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So shouldn't we have the final text of it? I mean, is this the final text? How do we know? If it's a proposal, it means that it still can be subject to changes before it becomes -- before it gets into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I agree entirely with you. But this is the -- the only document, unfortunately, that we have. And this is dated 8th of January, 1990. The witness became a chief of the CSB in April or May 1991. So by that time, this -- while we were proofing the witness, he recognised this -- this is just concerning the organisational structure of the CSB. And that is the only reason that I'm showing this to the witness, and the witness recognised during the proofing and he will testify to that, that this is the situation in the organisational sense that he found when he became the chief of the CSB. So, therefore, we can assume that this -- in this part, this proposal was accepted somewhere in the meantime between 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to say I am surprised that counsel for the other side wasn't on their feet. Because you -- it appeared to me that you were crossing the line into giving evidence, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't so much that. I don't think this is a particularly important point, Your Honour. But for future reference, to say with the witness with his headphones on listening to us, This is what the witness will say, is not, in my judgement, a very good way of going about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I understand. I was trying to be helpful. I didn't thought that this was in the point of contest between us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It isn't, Your Honours. But nonetheless, just for future reference, this is not a proper way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, and I'm sorry. [Microphone not activated]. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, what can you tell us about the content of this document, in terms of the organisational scheme and structure of the Security Services Centre, as you found it when you joined in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the organisational structure, this is what it was. There was the public -- public security centre, which had its departments. The first one was the department for the detection and prevention of crime; the police department; the administrative legal and personnel department; there was an anti-arson department; the department for finances; and there was also the state security sector with its own departments; and there was a common -- communications centre. And here you can see all the elements and who was doing what. If we are talking about individual departments, you see that their job descriptions are also given in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, when you are talking about the lines of work and when you listed them for us, along a certain hierarchy, did they go from the lowest structure, and when I mention the lowest structure I mean public security stations, up to the republican MUP. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in that, the police department in the centre had the role to organise and direct the work of police stations. They were not order issues [as interpreted]. However, the police administration in the ministry issued orders to the police in the centre. Their role was also instructive and supervisory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood your comment properly, this document which is the proposal for the regulation on internal organisation reflects the organisational situation that you found upon becoming chief of CSB in April and May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there's no objection, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, there are a number of questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I just checked. I withdraw my proposal because we actually have the -- in our law library, we have the whole ... it's P850. Sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That was the second question I was about to ask. The first question is coming back to the question Judge Delvoie asked. And I heard after the exchange what the witness said, but I'm still not clear as to the -- what is termed a proposal, on the one hand, and what he saw when he came in, on the other. Could you clarify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, just very briefly, please, explain to us the structure that existed at the Doboj CSB at the time when you became chief. If I may assist you further, please give us the description of how it was divided, both within public and state security lines of work and what were joined services.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was the department for public security and the department for state security. Each department was headed by a chief. The public security had the following structure: A crime detection and prevention section, within which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt, I think I got that when the witness said it initially. My question is a much simpler one, and it is whether -- despite the fact that we don't have, I suppose, a final version, whether, although called a proposal, this is it. That's -- that's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's obviously entirely my fault. The thing is that I -- I consulted -- we do have the final version and it's P850. It is -- it is a document which contains the actual -- the whole rule-book of the -- which was -- which was in force at the time. And that is why I withdrew this -- my proposal to admit this document. I'm sorry, I mis -- I misinterpreted Your Honours' wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then a last question just to understand it. It's not specifically -- but shouldn't this be an L number then, law library? It's a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am -- over the break, I can provide this answer because I ... I don't know at this point what is the explanation, why it not L but P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The explanation seems to be that this was tendered before we made an L category.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, you just enumerated public security stations which were branch stations of the CSB, and you gave us the names of their chiefs at the time. The only other remaining item that could be relevant would be ethnic background of the chiefs. So if you know this information, could you please tell us, listing each SJB and the ethnic background of their chief at the time.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Brod, Samac, Derventa, and Modrica, the chiefs were Croats, of Croat background. In Doboj and Teslic, the chiefs were Serbs. In Tesanj, Maglaj, the chiefs were of Muslim or Bosniak ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, at the time, in 1991, how did local policy-makers view your appointment as chief of the Doboj CSB?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the politicians were concerned, from the very beginning, I faced a sort of obstruction and disagreement with my appointment to that position due to the fact that I was apolitical at the time. I did not belong to any of the political parties which took part in the coalition government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best to illustrate this by way of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter of the Defence, 749D1, tab 1A, please. Dated 29th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. We're waiting for the English translation of the document. Yes, please go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This document was sent out to the field. As you can see in the heading, it says "Regional Board," or actually, that's at the bottom of the document. The Regional Board of the SDS. This document was sent to a number of addressees in all municipalities within the jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this document was also sent to the MUP headquarters and also to the Main Board of the SDS in Sarajevo, as well as to the SJBs in the Doboj region?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see exactly to whom it was addressed in the top of the document. I had some problems regarding this because -- where it says here that I was not their representative and did not have their support, and they were entitled to have their man in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain this to us in a bit more detail. Who was their man? Why did they formulate it in this manner? Would you please give us some background information and also explain the second page which is part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page of this document in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear here that, among three of us, three candidates for this post, the SDS had its favourite, which was Milan Ninkovic. After all of the procedures were completed, and once I was appointed to the post, they were displeased that their man was not appointed. At the SDS meeting, they adopted this decision, and they sent it to all of the addressees listed on the first page. However, the minister and the others who were together with Minister Delimustafic abided by their original decision. They did not want to amend it. However, in my work, in my further work, I faced constant problems with respect to these political structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, despite this intervention of the regional board of the SDS, which was sent to the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to its headquarters, it was therefore sent to the ministry which was headed at the time by Minister Alija Delimustafic, the ministry did not want to amend its initial decision to appoint you as chief of the CSB, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Bjelosevic, this, let's say, opposition against your appointment, was this normal procedure? Was this done by the rules? Was it in the rule, the possibility that the -- that this board could oppose and that the minister had -- had to reassess and eventually change his appointment or keep it as it was? So was it in the rules, or was this something extraordinary? Was this an unusual intervention of this board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that something of this nature was not set forth in the rules. However, there was a sort of a political agreement among the political parties which did not have a force of law or any other mandatory regulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify this, Mr. Bjelosevic, is it true that among national coalition parties, that is to say, the SDS, the SDA, and HDZ, there was a coalition agreement reached?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was also agreement on allocation of senior positions in all state agencies and structures, including the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that this agreement also entailed the duty on the part of the proposing party which was entitled, in accordance with the coalition agreement, to propose a candidate, a duty to propose three candidates so that the other two coalition parties would then be able to give their consent to appointment of one among these three candidates?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already told you, there was an inter-party coalition agreement, and none of us could have been proposed for a post without there being a prior political agreement regarding this, without there being a prior consent for these candidates. However, the parties usually had their favourite among the three candidates. Mr. Ninkovic was the favourite of the party, although they did consent to my candidacy and that of the third candidate. However, they preferred that Milan Ninkovic be appointed. This is why they sent this letter. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Bjelosevic. Let's clarify. You have to be clear in your answers. When you say "the party," are you referring to the SDS? If I understood you well, the SDS, which, according to the coalition agreement, was entitled to appoint the chief of the Doboj CSB, they proposed three candidates. That was their proposal. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I haven't objected so far, but each and every one of these questions was leading. There is not a lot of dispute about this. But I would ask that Mr. Zecevic is quite careful because he is actually literally putting words into the mouth of the witness. It's not what the witness said at all. Mr. Zecevic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm trying to save the time and sort of direct the witness. Because the witness is obviously inexperienced in giving a testimony, so that's why I'm crossing the line a bit and I'm fully aware of that, but I didn't thought that this was an issue that is contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, as you see, we have objections from the Prosecutor. So in order to avoid that, would you please explain in detail how that looked in practice in the case of Doboj. How come this document came about? How come you were the person appointed by the minister and not the person who was the SDS favourite?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: In respect of each and every post that was deemed to be important, an agreement had to be reached first among the coalition parties. And in this specific case, since there had been an agreement reached that the right of choice for the chief in this instance lay with the SDS, three candidates were put forth. Once the proposal is made, the party making the choice can choose any of the three. However, the case of the matter was that whenever any of the parties nominated their three candidates, they would have their favourite. In this particular instance, their favourite or, rather, their candidate number one wasn't the one that was chosen. Rather, it was me, and it was in this way that the party expressed their dissatisfaction with it. You see that they sent this memo to the presidents of the municipal assemblies present in the region, presidents of Executive Boards, the MUP of Sarajevo, and even to the chiefs of stations. In other words, individuals who were within the hierarchy below the chief of CSB and the Main Board of the SDS, they were the addressees. Still, the minister and whomever it was who made the choice with him stuck to me as being the one from among the three candidates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm still not clear about one detail. It all starts with the inter-party agreement, and that means that the parties agree upon the affiliation of the person to be appointed. It will be an SDS candidate or a candidate of the Muslim party or a candidate of the Croat party. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't based on party affiliations but on ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On ethnicity, okay. Okay. And then the three names within the ethnicity that had been chosen, were those three names -- was this list made upon the agreement between the parties? Was that a party agreement as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What remained was the right to challenge any of the candidates, if there was an underlying reason. For instance, in respect of some of the functions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The three -- the -- the parties had to agree on the candidates, on the three persons proposed by, in this case, the SDS. Is that right? So what -- what I wasn't sure about was whether the three parties had to be -- had to -- whether the parties had to agree on the three candidates, or that it was the right of the SDS to -- to propose three candidates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain this more broadly. Let's stick to the Security Services Centre. It was agreed amongst the parties that the chief of the centre would be a Serb. Specifically, the chief of the public security service in Doboj would be a Muslim, and the chief of the State Security Service would be a Croat. And that was the result of an inter-party agreement. Now, since every party basically clung to ethnicity itself, they each had the right to nominate three candidates, and they didn't have to seek the agreement of the other two parties for the three candidates. For instance, the SDS didn't have to seek the approval of the HDZ and the SDA in respect of its three candidates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So it was, in this specific case, the SDS who appointed three candidates. The other parties had nothing to say about that. But, still, within the three candidates, the SDS had a preference, which I can understand. But then they had the right to say, We want that candidate and not one of the other two. Why did they have to propose three candidates then? Why not just say, That's the one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the obligation to nominate at least three candidates. And there were many reasons why this was insisted on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, did the other coalition parties have the right to challenge the candidates put forth by one of the coalition parties?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that they did at this level. Or for this level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase the question this way. Mr. Bjelosevic, when you were nominated for the post of chief of CSB Doboj, did you enjoy the support of the Party of Democratic Action and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you -- what you mean, if I enjoyed their support.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. Did Alija Delimustafic, the then-minister, represent the Party for Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did Alija Delimustafic sign your candidacy?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did Alija Delimustafic -- or, rather, tell me, who was in charge of personnel issues within the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an administration for personnel. Hilmo Selimovic was the head. Later on there was a change.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Srebrenikovic. I can't recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it Mirsad?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Possibly. An individual, at any rate, who had not been living in Bosnia-Herzegovina before that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly, Mr. Bjelosevic. Hilmo Selimovic, who was the chief of the personnel administration within the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the individual who replaced him subsequently, Srebrenikovic, were both of them SDA cadres?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, the SDS Doboj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm sorry, but I am a little bit confused here. Or rather, aren't you confusing political parties and state authorities? The authority that has the power to nominate? Because you're talking about the minister and the head of the -- the head of the personnel service in the administration. And you -- you -- Could the witness remove his -- his headphones, please. And you -- if I understand you well, you're trying to suggest that this is a party challenge to the candidates proposed by the SDS. Is that a party challenge?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's the normal consequence of three candidates proposed to the government and the government taking a position, whether that government -- whether the minister is of this ethnicity or that ethnicity or the head of personnel is of this ethnicity or that ethnicity. So I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But that -- that's precisely the point, Your Honours, I'm trying to establish. The -- according to the coalition agreement between the parties, they have -- they have designated a certain system, or how it was understood which party is having the right to name its own candidates for a certain position within the government structures. For example, like this example, the chief of the CSB of Doboj. So according to the coalition agreement, it was the right of the SDS. And the witness explained that -- that the system existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But the right of the SDS was to -- to nominate three candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So where's the problem? It leaves a -- even in that -- in that coalition agreement, it leaves -- it leaves room for appreciation for the minister who has to nominate. It -- there are three SDS candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there are three SDS candidates, and that is sent -- the -- the system with the three was that -- the system was designated with the three so as that the other parties or the -- the actual minister or the -- the government authorities have the right to choose. But it is -- it is also understood, at least it is my understanding, that if the minister or the people who are choosing are of the -- of the certain -- are the representatives of the certain party, they do have, in their mind, the position of that particular party. And that's what I'm trying to establish with the witness. When taking the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say we're taking an awful long time over what seems to be a fairly simple point. But I do really want to reiterate my objection. Whatever Mr. Zecevic may believe is the case is not relevant. He can ask non-leading questions of the witness to establish what the witness's knowledge of this is, and then if he wants to call further evidence or point us to what evidence there is about it, that's something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, but I was invited by Their Honours to explain my position, and that is what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Every question has been a leading one to the witness. As it turns out, the witness isn't actually agreeing with you, and it may well be that the witness doesn't have the faintest idea. And if you ask it in a non-leading form, you may get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My impression, Mr. Zecevic, was that the witness clearly said that there was no possibility to challenge the -- the -- within the three names, possibility for the other parties to challenge the candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will -- I will give my explanation at the end, I guess. Otherwise, it would be -- it would be -- there would be an opposition from the Office of the Prosecutor. But there is a very clear answer to that, Your Honour. May I continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is this a convenient point to take the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will continue afterwards. We would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, who was it who ultimately signed your appointment to the chief of CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The then-minister, Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I wish to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours. But could I just ask, is this a document that was provided by Mr. Bjelosevic to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, we touched upon the structure of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina only briefly, and that at the time when you became the chief of CSB Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P875?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I'll ask you to give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Usher please assist me in giving the witness my folder to have a look. Can we please see it on the monitor, the whole breadth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can you give us your comments on this organigram of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period between January 1991 and March 1992 that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see this organigram from the minister down to assistant ministers to the various territorial units, including public security stations within the centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the names of assistant ministers who are divided up by their line of work? And can you confirm that this was, indeed, the case at the time, that these were the individuals who held these posts?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Alija Delimustafic was minister at the time. His assistant was Zepinic, as is reflected here, indeed. And then -- or, rather, his deputy was Zepinic. And then from assistants, yes, I do recognise these names, and I would say that this was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, can you explain to us what sort of situation existed on the ground when, in late April/early May, you took up the position of chief of the CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of organisation, the situation reflected this organigram. That's what it looked like. There was some change in the personnel at the time, but this was the result of previous agreements. However, as early as in 1991, there was a very complex security situation in the then-Yugoslavia, primarily because of the war in Croatia which began in early May, and with that conflict spreading. There emerged a wave of refugees in Croatia who were moving to our region, and when I say "to our region," I mean the Bijeljina [as interpreted] area. There were quite a few refugees arriving from Western Slavonia, specifically Grubisno Polje. Some of the refugees stayed in the region and others headed onto Serbia or, rather, Yugoslavia. Well, it was all Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here, at page 33, line 9, it says: "When I say 'our region,' I mean the Bijeljina region."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wanted to correct on the transcript. Can you tell us what was the ethnicity of the refugees you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The refugees arriving in the Doboj area were Serbs. There were some Croats among them, but most of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Another issue that was typical for that period of time was that quite a few individuals went from Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Croatian front line. This was also a cause of interethnic mistrust. Quite often it would so happen that members of all sorts of formations would come back from Croatia to their home areas in the Doboj region. They would come wearing uniforms, and they would often carry weapons as well. Fear was widespread among the population. In some places, there were instances of sabotage taking place. In particular, the bridge on the Vijaka river, between Derventa and Prnjavor, was blown up. This took place in September, sometime in September. It was a long time ago; I can't remember exactly. But I do believe it was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When say September, what year do have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: 1991. This caused some distress among the citizens in the area. And I know that very soon after that, the first guards appeared on the bridge across the Ukrina river because people feared for the safety of that bridge. They feared that it might be blown up as well, and that's why they guarded it at night. The position of that bridge is between the villages of Strpci and Detlak, near the fish pond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say guards, what guards do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean village guards. People who simply organised themselves, they took weapons that they had to hand, and they stood guard on both sides of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Bjelosevic, at that time, and I mean September 1991, were there any onslaughts by armed forces from the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: In September, if my memory serves me well, I believe it was on the 15th of September, 1991, an attack was launched at the barracks in Slavonski Brod, and that is across the river Sava from -- across Bosanski Brod, and during the state of Yugoslavia, Slavonski and Bosanski Brod functioned as one whole, as one unity. In the evening hours, that clash escalated into a proper armed combat. From the Slavonian side, fire was opened across the river towards the right bank, towards Bosanski Brod, primarily an engineering point of the Yugoslav People's Army that was there. And after that, there was mortar fire of a higher calibre, targeting the villages of Gisca [phoen], Klakar, both of them in the territory of Bosanski Brod municipality. At the Klakar brick-works we also had a victim, if I remember it properly. That person was an engineer. His name was Goranovic; I can't remember his first name, though. He was killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have to explain what you said on page 35.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 35, 1 and 2, can you explain what you said on that page? And I mean the situation involving Slavonski and Bosanski Brod settlements. You said that in the former Yugoslavia those two settlements functioned as one whole. Can you please explained geographical location of those two places, and what did you mean when you say that? It is not very clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I said that they functioned as one whole, I mean the organisation of health care in these two cities, I mean the education system, as well as the economy, of course. To this very day, this is an oil refinery in Bosanski Brod. Back then, about 800 people who worked in the refinery were from Slavonski Brod. In Slavonski Brod, there was a large factory whose name was Djuro Djakovic. It was a large industrial complex. A lot of people from Bosanski Brod commuted to Slavonski Brod and worked in that industrial complex. The hospital and all other health care institutions are funded -- were funded jointly by Bosanski and Slavonski Brod. Bosanski Brod didn't even have a maternity ward. That's what I meant when I said that the two cities functioned as one whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, those were two cities in two different republics separated by a river, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at document 117 -- or, rather, that's tab 117. 65 ter 758D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we go to that one. Mr. Bjelosevic, a few minutes ago you said that it would happen that members of all sorts of formations would come back from the -- from Croatia, the Croatian front, I suppose, to their homes, to their home areas in the Doboj region. They would come wearing uniforms and they would often carry weapons. They would come wearing uniforms and all different sort of formations, you said. Am I correct by the taking that, generally, the uniforms were JNA uniforms? Or would that be other uniforms as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, some wore JNA uniforms, those who belonged to JNA units. However, what I meant here were primarily members of the Croatian National Guards, the HOS units from Croatia, and other units that had been established there. People from Doboj region went and joined those units as volunteers. Therefore, the situation was such that we had members of the JNA as the regular military of Yugoslavia at the time, and, other hand, there are also members of those paramilitary units from Croatia who had returned in uniforms, often carrying weapons, and they would come back to our region. And that had quite a strong impact on creating distrust among ethnic groups and instilling fear among people. There were armed components from Croatia which clashed with the JNA in our immediate vicinity. Fear was rife and there was a lot of mistrust as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's an important clarification. I understand now that there were people from both sides fighting at the Croatian front in the same area in Doboj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, before we look at the document that I have just called up, and before I invite your comments, let me ask you this: Which of the municipalities in your region bordered on the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Brod, Odzak, Samac, and Derventa, partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it was just the river Sava that separated those municipalities from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 758D1 is the document that I would like to call up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please comment on this document. The title is report. The date is 14 September 1991, issued by the public security station in Bosanski Samac. The signatory is a certain Djordje Tesic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said tab number 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us something about this document, please, and about this case as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the incident. That was precisely one of those events that involved members of those formations who had arrived in Bosanski Samac. The police went to the place of the incident. As you can see from the document, they brought those armed men in. However, no criminal reports were ever filed. There was no prosecution against those men. As you can see in the document, the reason was that the chief of the police station in Bosanski Samac, Vinko Dragicevic, ordered that the individuals had their weapons returned and that they were released. Later on, that incident kept on being commented in town. It also instilled a certain degree of fear and mistrust, even among the members of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will come back to that situation in Samac. We will revisit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document. It is 65 ter -- it has been misrecorded. 65 ter 758D1. I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask, is this a document given by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Although I heard what the witness -- if I understood him correctly, that this incident formed the background to later comments that were made, I'm still not sure that I see how it assists, Mr. Zecevic. Could you assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely in relation to the -- to the answer that the witness gave to His Honour Judge Delvoie's question, about the -- the incidents created by people -- the members of the units from Croatia who came to the territory of -- of the region of Doboj and the CSB of Doboj, and the problems that that fact caused in the -- in the territory. That is precisely the document that confirms that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we look at the document under tab 2. 1D253, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, this is a dispatch already in evidence. You signed this dispatch, and you sent it out on the 16th of September, 1991. It was delivered to the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of to Bosnia-Herzegovina to the minister and deputy minister. What do you remember about the dispatch and its contents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is information about that armed incident. Or, rather, about the armed conflict that had taken place on the 15th of September. On the following day, we set up an investigation team. They went to inspect the place. They carried out an on-site inspection. They found mortar shell craters around the water works in Bosanski Brod, in Lijesce and around the Klakar brick-works. In the evening, on the day when the incident had taken place, and the incident was a major event, I spent some time in Bosanski Brod myself. I experienced the incident first-hand. I experienced fire being opened from all sorts of weapons. I dare say that that was already an attempt to transfer the armed conflict that had been taking place in Croatia into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this conflict that erupted on the 15th of September, 1991, was it the first such serious conflict in your area or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was the first serious conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 65 ter 760D1, tab 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, what was the impact of this conflict of 15th September in Bosanski Brod and in the entire region?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian side, from that time on, blocked the bridge. The bridge was mined and a check-point was established on the Croatian side in Slavonia. It wasn't allowed to have anybody cross from Bosanski Brod into Slavonski Brod, anybody without their passes. When I say "their," I'm referring to those from Slavonski Brod. This meant that people from Bosanski Brod could not go to Slavonski Brod to work there. However, the people from Slavonski Brod could cross over and come into Bosanski Brod. They could go to the refinery, to their work there. As a result of this ban on crossing from Bosanski Brod to Slavonski Brod, a lot of people were fired from their jobs, and consequently a protest was organised. The demands that people voiced during that protest meeting were quite clear. They wanted reciprocal measures to be introduced; that is to say, they either wanted that everybody be allowed to use the bridge, all citizens of Bosanski Brod and Slavonski Brod, or that the bridge be closed off for everyone. This is why I sent a dispatch regarding this to the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as to the deputy prime minister for internal policy, as well as to the minister and deputy minister. I believe this to be an important incident with serious consequences for the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the citizens of Bosanski Brod, and I also thought that I needed to provide first-hand information to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is what this dispatch of yours is about. The dispatch of the 30th of September, 1991, that we can see on the screens now, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm assuming, Your Honours, unless otherwise stated, that all of these documents come from the witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not all of them, but this one does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I will now show you 65 ter 759D1, tab 3. And I would like you to comment on it. Could you please explain this document to us and tell us, if you remember, what prompted Minister Delimustafic to send this dispatch. What was the event?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I remember this dispatch. I think that it was written, inter alia, due to the conduct of the chief of the station in Brod, in Bosanski Brod. There was some information indicating that when it came to this incident, it was first the Crisis Staff and the police administration in Slavonski Brod that were informed about it, and only subsequently and in a limited volume was the information sent to the MUP in Sarajevo and to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. When you say "information," are you referring to the information from the Bosanski Brod SJB, from the Bosnian side which was subordinated to you, the Doboj centre. Is that -- is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, later on, I learned that there was a special telephone line set up, of which we knew nothing at the time. The telephone line between the police administration in Slavonski Brod and the SJB station in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just one moment. Your previous question - let's clarify this - and the answer, is that to say that the transcript of the previous answer is wrong, where it is referred to Slavonski Brod and not to Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely why I wanted to clarify that, because I see that there is some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There was some -- something illogical --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- some problems in understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the reference to Slavonski Brod is not correct. It was not that this information was first sent to the -- to the Crisis Staff and the police administration in Slavonski Brod. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that is correct. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Witness, if I understand the next answer correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I said and I will repeat, that the chief of the public security station in Bosanski Brod first got in touch and sent information to Slavonski Brod, to the police administration in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... demonstration, I think, of please, please, let the witness answer the questions and not counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when I said "correct," I meant that the witness's answer was correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, please, you have to understand that we, including myself, are not very familiar with the situation you are describing. Is it true that Slavonski Brod is in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Bosanski Brod is a town in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was your reply that the chief of police in Bosanski Brod - that is to say, a town in Bosnia - first informed the Crisis Staff of the town in Croatia and their police administration before informing the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this call to Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of the police station relied on Slavonski Brod outside of the rules and contrary to the hierarchy, outside of the hierarchy. Simply speaking, he slowly was turning himself in the direction of Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But if I understand it correctly, the attack came from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So when the chief of SJB in Bosanski Brod called his colleague on the other side, was that to stop the attack or ... why -- what was the purpose of the call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, there already existed a certain amount of co-ordination, and there were plans between certain people in the Bosanski Brod police station and the police administration in Slavonski Brod. That is to say, there was a parallel structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what were these plans about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, later on, it will be implemented, in a way. That is to say, that Croatian forces, with the assistance of certain paramilitary forces from Bosanski Brod, would occupy the SJB in Bosanski Brod, all key positions in Bosanski Brod, and, later on, the wider area of the territory of Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So am I right to conclude that -- that the communication between the two SJBs on each side of the river was really designed to have the chief of the SJB on the Bosnian side in Bosanski Brod, to facilitate the attack and the possible subsequent takeover of Bosanski Brod by forces from Croatia. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. This wasn't at all clear to me, but ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just raise something about this whole line of -- and perhaps the witness should take off his earphones for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I haven't stopped this so far, but at the moment I'm not clear at all how -- how this is relevant to the issues which Your Honours have to deal with. Your Honours, I don't certainly want to have spend any time dealing with this area of the conflict which is not part of our indictment, and, of course, what you're getting, not surprisingly, is one side of it. And I could spend, clearly, if I wanted to, and I fully appreciate that, in cross-examination, time dealing with the other aspect of this part of the conflict. But it seems to me at the moment I'm not clear how that is going to assist Your Honours in any way in arriving at a decision on the events which are related to this indictment. I merely raise it at this stage. If Your Honours feel that, you know, this is helpful, then I will sit down. But, at the moment, I'm saying the relevance to the issues which Your Honours have to deal with is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I? [Interpretation] Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. [In English] Okay. I will speak in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is obviously -- and I'm afraid I forgot about that. His microphone -- he can hear through the earphones even when they're like that. They're turned up quite loud. I'd forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- Your Honours, I didn't -- I didn't plan to use this much time before on -- on this. I think this is significant because this is the first really serious armed conflict that happened in the territory of the CSB where -- where our witness was chief of the CSB, and this is the last document I have on that, and I don't have any more questions. Because this is how I'm bringing you to the context of what is happening and what repercussions this incident had on the -- on the structure of the CSB which is, of course, very relevant for the -- for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think I follow that, Mr. Zecevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear interpretation? Fine. You've explained to us that the order which we have before us is the response from the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to what happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there is no objection to the document, I would like to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, following these events in September 1991, what sort of bearing did these events and the general atmosphere have on the workings of the CSB Doboj, in terms of their dealings with public security stations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was already at this time that the system began collapsing, if I may say so; the system of management and the hierarchy itself within the MUP. Certain paramilitary formations came into being already at this time in our regions, and, as a result, there was fear, there was growing fear, and there was also a growing mistrust between the various ethnicities. There was a sort of differentiation which was occurring on the ground and becoming ever more serious.
