In retrospect, it seems to me that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina failed to respond properly to this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is: What sort of consequences, if any, the situation had for the functioning of CSB Doboj? And I mean in professional terms.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, negative consequences, by all means. The subordination system, the reporting system that existed within it began to collapse. It was disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "negative consequences," and the information or reporting system that you mention, was this the only aspect of it that you could experience within the CSB or was there more to it than that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the situation as it existed in the field, that was the extent of it. But if we look at it more broadly, and if we look at what sort of relations there existed between the ministry and the centre, as well as the stations that were present within the centre, that's where things get even more complicated. Some of the stations would establish direct communication with the personnel administration where it came to personnel issues. Some of the chiefs of stations were appointed in violation of some of the regulations envisaged under the state administration law. Gradually, it all gained the hallmarks of a shadow, parallel, system which caused the entire system to be undermined.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically: You, as the chief of CSB, were you, under the rules of service and under the law, supposed to be informed of the appointments made to the various posts within the stations in your area?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the standard procedure was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed and consulted of these issues; and, if so, can you give us specific examples?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't consulted on these issues. And I can give you an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The appointment of the chief of public security station in Derventa, for instance, where Ivan Duspara was appointed chief, an individual who did not meet the requirements under the -- prescribed under the state administration law where it came to his educational background and the requisite qualifications. At a later stage, he would directly apply to the personnel administration, visit there, and bring along the decisions on the assignment of policemen to various areas without applying the standard procedure which was that the administration was supposed to be contacted via the CSB. He would, instead, go directly to the personnel administration with all the relevant documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you inform the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of such occurrences? Did you intervene in that sense?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I even asked for Mr. Duspara to step down after he was appointed, precisely by stating all these underlying reasons. But there were other examples, such as the one involving the deputy chief of state administration in Doboj, where, again, the standard procedure was not applied. So I drew their attention to this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 764D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, Mr. Zecevic's question was, a few minutes ago: "Let me ask you specifically: You, as the chief of CSB, were you, under the rule of service and under the law, supposed to be informed of the appointments made to the various posts within the stations in your area?" The question was informed. You said yes. And then the discussion went on, not only to the point to know whether you were informed but also to the point to know whether you were consulted. So my question is: Under the rule of law, was there an obligation to consult you or only to inform you after appointment? To consult you before the appointment; or to inform you after appointment? Or both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the Law on State Administration, the degree and profile of professional qualifications for each and every post was provided. This was further explored through various rule-books, which set out the procedure under which, for instance, the chief of CSB was to be appointed, or the chief of public or state security sectors. In these two cases that I referred to, both the Law on State Administration was broken and -- or, rather, because the requirement for the post of chief of CSB was that of post-secondary school degree. This wasn't met. And this was also a violation of the procedure that was in place which made it incumbent on them to consult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To consult. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To consult and to send the proposal or the candidacy once it's been agreed upon, to be sent to the ministry from the CSB, and this wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My very specific question was: According to the rules, did you, as CSB chief, have to be consulted before a chief of SJB was appointed in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was supposed to be consulted, and under the rule-book, it was the CSB that was supposed to send out the proposal to the personnel administration of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, I said "consulted" in the first place but it was -- it was -- it was translated -- interpreted as "informed." But never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, let us clarify this. Did you, or did the chief of CSB submit the official proposal to the ministry for appointments to chiefs -- to the posts of chiefs of SJBs as provided for under the rules and regulations of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in these instant cases, that's not how it happened and it should have, indeed, happened in such way that these proposals would go out -- would be submitted from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, under the rules, it should have been done this way; but, in reality, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the reason why you intervened?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours. Maybe this is the proper time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We would return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I requested a document, 764D1. It's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, before you is a document dated the 24th of October, 1991. And I think that you signed it. Can we have your comments on the document? What's it about? It's behind tab 7 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely my response to the violation of regulations and procedures where change in personnel was concerned. That's precisely what we were discussing a moment ago. These are the issues that undermined the very system of work. You see that there are instances of direct communication contrary to the laws and procedures in place, as well as appointments, et cetera. And the consequences are clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this your memo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And who was it sent to, who was it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the minister of the interior and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there no objections, I would like to have this document admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, how does this assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness -- the last 15 minutes of the previous session we were talking about the situation in the SJB and the actual non-compliance with the laws at the time on appointments of the chiefs of the SJB. The witness said he informed and was protesting that with the MUP of SRBiH and here is the document that confirms that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So this supports the fact that he complained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's your purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the witness said: I filed a complaint and this is the actual document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, what was the security-related situation like in the area covered by the centre in the course of autumn 1991, if you can tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was very complex. As of roughly the month of September, things grew gradually worse, due to the events we discussed; various instances of sabotage, the bridge being destroyed, conflicts between the forces of the National Guard Corps and the army, and the spilling over of these conflicts to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the emergence of paramilitary forces in our area as well, the arming and organising of paramilitary structures. Naturally, all this made up for a very complex security situation. To confirm that this was, indeed, the case, we have the statement by Sefer Halilovic, who was the first commander of the staff of the BH army, who confirmed, in one of the interviews he gave for the BH TV, that as of September, October, and by early November, around 60 per cent of the work surrounding the formation of these units had already been completed. We took notice of that, and the MUP, both along its public and state lines, was being notified of it, but the situation grew increasingly complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the statement given for the television, was this something that you yourself saw or heard?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in June 2009, I believe. He was explaining how things were happening, what the objective was, how they frequently changed the location of their staff, precisely in order to maintain the secrecy of the exercise, and we -- those of us who were out in the field were aware of these events. However, we had -- we didn't have the power to confront it, because by then it had gained momentum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Bjelosevic, "we were aware," does it mean that you were aware of the situation back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew back then, thanks to the information we had from the state security sector, and we also had some information that we received from the JNA. We exchanged information. And what happened next confirmed that these sentiments were more or less true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'm getting slightly confused about the dates. I think there's an error, certainly, in line 25 of page 54, which reads: "Sometime in June 2009." And Mr. Zecevic has just asked: "Were you aware of the situation back in 1992?" I thought it was 1991 we were talking about. But, in any event that line 25 must clearly not -- is clearly not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when did you hear Sefer Halilovic's statement on BH television, as you put it, and which period did it refer to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 2nd of June, 2009, that Sefer Halilovic made the statement in a TV show.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that was in 2009. But it referred to the situation as it prevailed in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, Mr. Bjelosevic, what sort of measures did the MUP and CSB take in the course of 1991, in view of the highly complex security situation? And were any measures taken at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the complex situation and developments at the time, we were under the obligation to inform the ministry headquarters of all these events, and we did as much. So it went beyond the usual reporting of crime which follow falls under the purview of either a station or a centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, did you take any specific measures; and, if so, which?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: We informed the ministry of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in autumn of 1991, did you set up check-points at intersections?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was an activity that had been agreed with the Federal Secretariat for National Defence of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Certain check-points were set up at key intersections and on the points of entry into Bosnia-Herzegovina. The check-points were manned by mixed personnel, meaning civilian and military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of activity was going on at these check-points? What were their duties?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the task was precisely to heighten the control of movement of paramilitary formations, of arms smuggling, illegal arming, foreign currency smuggling, and any activities that had the hallmarks of subversive activities or sabotage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which specific measures did members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina apply at these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Their activity was regulated by instructions, and the military police had the control over military and paramilitary personnel; whereas, members of the MUP controlled vehicles, whether they were stolen vehicles or not, and did all the other policing duties within the MUP purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I'm asking you very specifically what measures were taken. Do you know or do you not know what measures were taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Illegal cars were confiscated, people were brought in and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, did you check the IDs of people who passed through those check-points?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We controlled car papers, and we checked people's IDs when we deemed necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you search the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were such activities taking place in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the entire territory. On main roads, cross-roads, and at the entry points into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that action had its name, as it were, or a title?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the name of the action was Check-point 91, or Point 91, if I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you please repeat about that action, Point 91, which members and of which services and organs participated in that action known as Point 91?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs of Yugoslavia, the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and JNA members. If I may add, that we, on the ground, received a letter from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That letter was signed by the minister, and in that letter, he informed us that that action or that activity would be taking place, and he also told us that we should provide assistance and information to the inspectors from the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please look at a document 65 ter D766, or D1, that's under tab 9. 766D1. Tab 9.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is information drafted by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, reporting the results that were achieved in the Point 91 operation. In the introduction, there is reference to the goals. The information was drafted on the 15th of November, 1991. And here you can see a list of all the results, as well as certain problems which were encountered on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We can only see the front page. How long is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D450 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in autumn 1991, were MUP reservists mobilised; and, if they were, on whose orders?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The reserve force was mobilised. I can't remember exactly on what date. And it was done on the order of the minister of the interior, Mr. Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As we have heard, you worked at the Secretariat for National Defence, and previously you were the chief of the Security Services Centre. Could you give us some technical details of mobilisation. When you wanted to mobilise the reserve force of the police, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had defence plans for every public security station which defined the number of people and the number of police stations in every specific municipality. A request was sent for a certain number of people to replenish wartime units. In the centres, there was a division for wartime preparations, and in the public security stations, there was a desk officer in each of the stations that dealt in those things. And in keeping with the plans, we mobilised a certain number of units to bring -- a certain number of men to bring units up to the strength. There was a mobilisation plan, a plan according to which men were mobilised. Reserve policemen would be issued with uniforms in a timely manner. They would take those uniforms home. In every wartime police station, there was a certain number of official IDs, exactly the number that was needed by the wartime police station for all its men. Those IDs, however, did not contain any personal data because the personnel changed all the time. The numerical strength remained the same, however. In case reserve police stations were activated, those IDs would have been issued to those men that were at the stations at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the reserve police were mobilised, did the mobilised police reserve officers also get weapons? Were they issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991, they were issued with weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- just one moment. Mr. Bjelosevic, this is a mobilisation order by the Minister Delimustafic. Was this mobilisation order specific to the Doboj CSB area; or was it a nation-wide mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that mobilisation applied to the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That it was carried out across the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, in autumn 1991, were there any visits to your Security Services Centre by anybody from the federal SUP, from their inspectors?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did come. Before the check-points were set up, in keeping with the minister's order, we informed federal inspectors about the current security and safety situation. Later on, they occasionally paid us visits when they wanted to analyse some things together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at 763D1, tab 6. Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the dispatch in question that was sent by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina announcing the arrival of federal inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, our LiveNote seems to have stopped working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Has it come up yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's in progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if that means it's going to come back at some stage or ... or what exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you so handicapped as Mr. Zecevic ought not to proceed. That is the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The trouble is I've lost -- if he could repeat for me the document tab number because that didn't come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I can proceed because we have the LiveNote on the monitor. It's on our computers we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Can you see the transcript, though, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So we can proceed, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you started talking about the document. Can you finish, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We, as chiefs of Security Services Centres, were given some tasks and obligations. We were asked to brief the federal inspectors about the security situation in the -- in the area and to put in place conditions for the functioning of those check-points in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D441, Your Honours. And page 59, line 1, exhibit number is 1D440. I misspoke; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please look at 765D1, tab 8. I would like to invite you to comment upon this order. Who signed it, first of all? Could we please look at the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: The document was signed by the minister of the interior, Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this dispatch for us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order for us to prepare, and it also gives us all the elements that we should include into our briefing session with the federal inspectors. There are bullet points for us to prepare ourselves, and that's what we followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this order connected with the previous order that we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this order elaborate your obligations with regard to the visit of those inspectors from the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It provides a lot more detail than the previous one. It actually gives a list of all the things that we needed to prepare in advance and how we should brief the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just been informed by my colleagues that they still don't have LiveNote. I don't know whether that presents any problems for Ms. Korner or the Prosecution. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think she's indicated that she doesn't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, what measures did the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina take or put in place in the course of 1991, with regard to the situation? More specifically, in your CSB and probably across Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the check-points or the overall situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The overall situation. We have already discussed the check-points.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to say that the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not undertake adequate measures, measures that would be adequate with respect to the problems that arose in the area at the time. I even had a feeling - and I also have some arguments to support this - that Operation Check-point 1991, which had given good results, is something that they did not like, and very soon they started obstructing that operation. I would especially like to highlight the arrival of inspectors from the MUP headquarters in Sarajevo. They had been sent by the headquarters to the area of the CSB Doboj. Contrary to some rules, these inspectors were sent to public security stations; first and foremost, Bosanski Brod and Bosanski Samac. The inspectors moved some check-points, as well as the personnel, policemen who manned the check-points. We provided policemen from the level of the Doboj CSB, and once these inspectors from the police administration arrived, as well as from other centres, those who had been sent, these police forces were sent back; whereas, they selected policemen from some other centres and brought them to Samac, and later on, to Bosanski Brod as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your answer. Who sent the inspectors from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; when did they arrive? And you also mentioned that it was contrary to some rules. Would you elaborate on that, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Normally, when the inspectors from the administration come to the centre, or to a station, they are typically announced, and they come either to conduct supervisory inspection of the work of the centre or the station, or they come in order to provide certain instructions. In this particular case, first of all, they were not announced. They did not bring them any kind of an order, be it from the minister, from assistant minister, or deputy minister. They simply came and said they came to conduct some co-ordination activities, as they termed it initially. As the time passed, I asked that they either produce an order on sending them to us, or a plan of work that they were supposed to conduct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Zecevic's microphone be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive it from them, and then, later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the interpreters need you to switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not produce either of the two documents that I asked for, and this is when I asked from the ministry that an explanation be given for their visit. It took several written interventions of mine --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the documents and you can continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 768D1, tab 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jusuf Pusina sent a dispatch at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we have a document on our screens. Would you please comment and tell us whose document it is and explain the background of the document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I sent this document to the minister, to the deputy minister, and to the then-Executive Council, to the deputy prime minister for internal policy, and to the president of the Assembly. In this memo I describe the problem, the one that I have just told you about, because the visit of the inspectors meant an introduction of a parallel system in the territory under the jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB. They directly interfered in the work of the centre, in the management of the centre. They took over the SJBs and sent separate reports bypassing the centre which, in a way, meant that the centre was almost suspended in all of its work and it meant that a parallel system was established. There is another matter that I wish to bring to your attention; namely, that all of these inspectors who had come, and there were a total of six of them staying there, were of Muslim ethnicity and that this produced a reaction, both in the SJBs that they visited, as well as among the population in the area. Because it disturbed further an already bad ethnic composition among the senior management and senior levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "bad ethnic composition in the senior management," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a rule that if a chief of SJB was of one ethnicity, then the commander of that SJB was supposed to be of a different ethnicity. And depending on what the composition of the population was, whether there were two ethnic communities or three ethnic communities, if it was a multi-ethnic community, then the third senior position was supposed to be given to a member of the third ethnic community. And the inspectors, with their arrival, disturbed this agreement. And especially once the police forces were brought in from elsewhere. That further disturbed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the problems that you just spoke about, the fact that the agreement, the structure was disturbed, that a parallel system was introduced, that the command and hierarchy in MUP was suspended and that basically the CSB became powerless. All of these things that you just described to us, were those the reasons why you sent this memo or were there other reasons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely those reasons, the ones that I have described to you. This is what prompted me to send this memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And to whom was this memo sent?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believed that the problem was quite a major one, and this is why I sent this memo to the minister of the interior, to his deputy, and to the Executive Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the deputy prime minister who was in charge of internal policy, and this was a problem from that domain, and I also sent the memo to the president of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This memo of yours that was just introduced into evidence, did it produce a response?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive a response, either from the minister or from his deputy. Rather, I received a reply from Mr. Jusuf Pusina. And to this day, I have a dilemma whether Mr. Pusina was able to intercept these memos before they reached the minister and the deputy, or whether the minister and the deputy allowed him, on purpose, to correspond with me so as to avoid any responsibility on their part for such a major problem. And I thought this was a major problem. This had long-ranging consequences for further work in the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 769D1, tab 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a reply, signed by Mr. Jusuf Pusina, a reply to my questions, to the questions I raised. As I have said, I did not receive a reply either from the minister or his deputy. In this reply, there is no information on who decided to send inspectors to Bosanski Samac and Bosanski Brod. Rather, this reply says that it was the ministry as an institution that did it. And this is why I had this dilemma; that is to say, it wasn't either the minister or the deputy that made this decision. Nor does he say that he, Jusuf Pusina, as assistant, made that decision. Rather, the document speaks of the ministry as a whole that made the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive, via this document or via contacts with Mr. Jusuf Pusina, any other obligations? Were you informed of any other obligations you had in relation to the inspectors who had come from the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: They asked for a car to be placed at the disposal of Omer Stambolic as well as a policeman who would be his security detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Zecevic's microphone be switched off when not in use, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be Exhibit 1D444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please comment on the next document. 65 ter 770D1, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I -- I can't help just making the comments that I think the Chamber is, by now, well-informed through the witness of the situation and the various attempts from the witness to the ministry to control the situation that evolved slowly by the end of 1991. So I don't know for how much longer you wish to pursue this -- this matter, but I think it's -- it's pretty clear the picture that emerges from what we have heard so far and what we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I believe that during our Defence case, we need to show -- I don't know whether I should switch into English and have the witness take off the headphones so as to avoid any perception that I'm giving instructions to him. Would you please switch off your mikes? [In English] The point, Your Honours, is the following. The allegation which was presenting during the Office of the Prosecutor's case is that -- that there was a joint criminal enterprise existing in -- starting to exist in October 1991, and one of the aspects of it was the -- was the meeting in the -- on the 11th of February in Banja Luka. The witness was present on that meeting in Banja Luka. Now, I'm trying to establish now why, what were the reasons why the witness and other people of Serbian ethnicity went to that meeting in Banja Luka on the 11th of February and try to establish that this was actually the only way they could cope with the -- with problems that they have experienced in their work in the ministry of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the level of inconsistencies of -- of misuse of the -- of the police force and the -- and the work, not in accordance with the laws and the regulations, was such that it justified the meeting and the topics that were discussed at that meeting. That is the aim. And since we have the original documents from that time, I -- I think only -- only proper way that would be that I introduce these documents with a comment of the person who received these comments [sic] and went, ultimately, to that meeting on the 11th of February. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I have to say is can I just confirm that all of these documents, again, are ones provided by Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, some were disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When Ms. Korner says "all of them," I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can see ones with ERNs which are clearly from us. But ones without ERNs, I'm taking it are produced by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me consult, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was just informed by my assistant that there are a number of documents which we uploaded and then they were given the ERN numbers afterwards and then returned to us from the Office of the Prosecutor side. But, Ms. Korner, Ms. Savic will give you the explanation to the detail, why she claims this is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, I think everything we've seen so far, either documents that the witness generated or received by him whether -- or otherwise that he could speak to authoritatively. So I don't -- the apprehension that is implicit in Ms. Korner's question --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, no, can I explain why I'm asking this each time. This, as you all know -- I'd ask the witness to take his earphones off. As Your Honours know because it has been uploaded, this interview -- this witness was interviewed in 2004. I would think about 1/20th of the documents which are now emerging from him were actually provided to us in that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, the witness was interviewed on both occasions as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But his lawyer turned up, who was present, as Mr. Zecevic knows, with a selected handful of documents. That's why I'm asking on each occasion to confirm that this is what he has now provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question was that you should clarify this document behind tab 12, 770D1. Can we have your comments on it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is yet another document drafted by Mr. Pusina following a number of interventions insisting on receiving answers to the question as to why the inspectors were sent, who, upon their arrival there, took charge of what was happening in these stations and in -- in a way, in the centre as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Zecevic please switch his microphone off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The suggestion was that he should assign a technical secretary to work with me, although there was a civil servant who had been working there previously but she was on maternity leave. In this letter, Mr. Pusina said that what was done was done under the instructions from the minister. I had asked on several occasions that I get in touch with Minister Delimustafic because I wanted to talk to him about this issue. I wanted to have a direct contact with him. No answer was forthcoming. Let me emphasise that throughout that time, which was almost a year, Minister Delimustafic did not hold a single meeting of the collegium to which he would invite all the chiefs of centres and which would have enabled us to discuss the problem together and which would have enabled us to report on the events taking place on the ground directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the document admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please have a look at document 771D1, which is tab 13. It has to do with the same issue, so can you please explain what it was about.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my dispatch which I sent to the minister and his office, to his deputy, to Assistant Jusuf Pusina and to Assistant Momcilo Mandic. The purpose of the letter was to provide them with information, since the situation in the two municipalities, namely, Samac and Bosanski Brod, were quite dramatic by that time. I drew their attention to -- or, rather, alerted them to what might follow. There might be unrest, protests, et cetera. I asked that they withdraw Mr. Stambolic from Doboj because he was suspended at the time as there was a disciplinary procedure pending against him, and here I state, yet again, my dilemma as to whether Minister Delimustafic was aware of it all or not. I tried to repeatedly to notify him of these problems directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bjelosevic, if my understanding is correct. The inspector who was sent out from the MUP headquarters, Stambolic, this one Omer Stambolic, your impression was that at the time he was in the area of your CSB, there was a disciplinary procedure pending against him and that he was, in fact, suspended?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Zecevic. I would like to ask the witness to read, in Serbian, the sentence: "For the above reasons, the police officers sent to Bosanski Samac," and so forth, and so on. Could you read that in Serbian, please? "For the above reasons the police officers sent to the Bosanski Samac SJB," and to the end of the sentence so that we'll get a translation of what you are reading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "For the above-mentioned reasons, the policemen who were posted or sent to the SJB Bosanski Samac will be withdrawn from their service in the SJB Bosanski Samac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Bjelosevic, I have a -- pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question is this: When it says, "For the above reasons the police officers will be withdrawn," are you asking the minister to withdraw them, or are you -- or is this your decision to withdraw them? It's a little bit confusing in -- in the context of the dispatch. What do you mean by "they will be withdrawn"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The composition of the police personnel that arrived from other areas included policemen from the stations under the Doboj centre. While those mixed check-points were still in effect, in other words, while the Punkt 91 or Check-point 91 operation was still ongoing, the situation was brought under control. The tensions eased and the security situation in general took a turn for the better significantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for just one moment. The police officers sent to Bosanski Samac is not referring to Hodzic and Panjek? It is referring to the other police officers that they brought to Bosanski Samac; is that right? So that's where my misunderstanding was. Those police officers that -- this is not referring to Hodzic and Panjek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And this is your decision to withdraw those extra policemen who did not come from Bosanski Samac. It is your decision to withdraw them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To avert the protests that were announced. We wanted to avoid having mass-scale unrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that's clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll look at one other document before we stop for today. 779D1, behind tab 15. Tab 15. This is another document by Mr. Pusina. Can we have your comments on it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC
utterances.text: This letter did not change the situation substantially or solve it. Yet again, Mr. Pusina sends out inspectors in their stead. As you can see Jusuf Vatres from the Sarajevo CSB is going do come; whereas, we do have inspectors within the police service of the CSB Doboj. Obviously there was something that they wanted to achieve with this, which only he and his associates were privy to, although it wasn't difficult to draw conclusions. Panjeta would be leaving, therefore, and he would be replaced by Inspector Jusuf Vatres. So they would change, but the ethnic structure, the ethnic makeup would remain roughly the same as would the duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I'd ask that the document be admitted. And I would stop here for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you, having been sworn -- we're about to take the adjournment for today and we'll resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Having been sworn as a witness in this matter, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side, the side that's calling you or the side that is examining you, until after you would have been released by the Chamber. Furthermore, in such communication as you may have with persons -- anybody outside of the Chamber apart from counsel, you cannot discuss your testimony. Do you understand what I just said? So you're now excused to return tomorrow morning at 9.00. We take the adjournment for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise one technical administrative matter. Ms. Savic has very kindly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may the witness be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the witness can go [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Usher, yes. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Savic has kindly pointed out that some of the documents we've notified to use for cross-examination are already on their list. We attempted to do a check. Theirs don't have ERN numbers in the same -- so we can't check against ERN numbers unless, quite by chance, they have them and there are many copies of the same document. But their spreadsheet does not have the date. We put the date on all of ours, and the -- and apparently the reason is because that wasn't a requirement, but it makes it easier when we're looking at their list to prevent us trying to put in the same documents and, therefore, having double exhibits if the column -- there's a column added to their spreadsheet which has the date. It's still not perfect, but it will make it easier for us to try and check against the two, because, otherwise, we are going to have -- end up with us trying to exhibit the same document that's already been a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the document's date is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there's a -- at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- in the document's description is in the wrong -- in the wrong column.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It makes it more difficult to search. Where if you've got a date, you can just simply search and see if the dates are the same. I mean, as I say, I don't think it's going to be perfect, but it'll help. And the reason I'm raising it with you is because I understand your only order was that it should be -- the 65 ter number, or whatever, so I'd ask that it simply includes the date. It may not even need an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So this is something we could leave to the attorneys to sort out outside the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I -- the reply came [indiscernible] I'm raising it. And, Your Honours, there's one other thing and I raise it -- simply, Your Honours, may recall that each and every one of our witnesses, before they started their evidence, was given a warning about the consequences of perjury, as it so happens, wherever this witness is -- our witnesses came from. That warning wasn't given, and I merely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The oversight is entirely mine. Thanks for the reminder, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would see that whether, practically speaking, it is something that I can correct or patch tomorrow morning before the witness resumes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, I only raised it because we just noted it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of April, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
